extracted.intended_audience: students, clinicians, and general readers interested in psychoanalysis and psychotherapy
extracted.subtask_description: Overview of psychoanalytic theory, indications/contraindications, techniques, training, cultural adaptation, and evidence standards for clinical practice. Summarizes what makes cases suitable for analysis, core analytic methods, variations in technique, training/accreditation expectations, and empirical evaluations of effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagnostic distinctions between psychosis, borderline, and antisocial
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychotic individuals: deficits in autonomous ego functions (e.g., 'loose associations,' 'blocking,' 'flight of ideas,' 'verbigeration,' 'thought withdrawal') and impaired development of self and object representations; show limitations in warmth, empathy, trust, identity, closeness and/or stability in relationships. Borderline patients: more intact reality testing but deficits in controlling impulses, affects, or fantasies. Adults who do not experience guilt and shame and who indulge in criminal behavior are usually diagnosed as psychopaths/antisocial personality disorder (DSM-IV-TR).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these functional/relational and reality-testing features to differentiate diagnoses and to guide treatment selection (e.g., borderline vs psychotic adaptations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Etiology and character of neurotic symptoms
rubrics_metrics.description: Neurotic symptoms (panic, phobias, conversions, obsessions, compulsions, depressions) are typically caused by intrapsychic conflicts among sexual and hostile-aggressive wishes, guilt and shame, and reality factors, rather than by deficits in ego functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that such conflicts may be conscious or unconscious and are managed by defensive operations like 'repression' and 'isolation of affect'; neurotic symptoms may co-occur with or without ego/object relations deficits, complicating diagnosis and treatment choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patient suitability/indications for psychoanalysis
rubrics_metrics.description: To be treated with psychoanalysis the person 'must demonstrate a desire to start an analysis,' have some capacity for speech and communication, and be able to have or develop trust and insight within the psychoanalytic session. A preliminary stage of treatment is required to assess amenability to analysis and to allow the analyst to form a working psychological model.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analyst decides suitability based on indications, pathology, and the 'fit' between analyst and patient; evaluation may include other analysts' opinions and discussion of financial/insurance issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Contraindications and special precautions (including severe suicidality and psychosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Severely suicidal patients may require a longer preliminary stage, sometimes with sessions that include a twenty-minute break, and may require hospitalization and psychotropic medication. Classical analysis is modified or supportive techniques are used for psychotic and near-psychotic patients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For patients lacking desire to explore root causes, analysis is contraindicated; modified forms (supportive therapy, medication, reality discussions) are indicated when ego functions are severely compromised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classical analytic technique components
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical technique comprises instructions (telling the patient to try to say what's on their mind, including interferences), exploration (asking questions), and clarification (rephrasing and summarizing what the patient has been describing). Confrontation may be used to bring defenses to the patient's attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These core procedural elements structure sessions and support interpretive work; practitioners may vary application depending on patient needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation methods and aims
rubrics_metrics.description: Primary method is interpretation of the patient's unconscious conflicts interfering with current functioning. Specific interpretation types include dynamic interpretation, genetic interpretation, resistance interpretation, transference interpretation, dream interpretation, and reconstruction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretations aim to connect unconscious conflicts to present symptoms (e.g., explaining how being 'too nice' guards against guilt) and to help the patient reorganize thought after insight; choice of interpretation is theory- and case-dependent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free association, couch setting, and handling resistance/transference
rubrics_metrics.description: When the patient reclines on a couch with the analyst out of view, the patient tends to remember more, experiences more resistance and transference, and is able to reorganize thoughts after insight – facilitated by interpretive work. Resistances revealed in errors, forgettings, and peculiarities about time/fees/talking signal unconscious avoidance of thought flow ('free association').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the setting and attention to resistances/transference to uncover unconscious material; clinicians should actively interpret resistances rather than treat silence as therapeutic in itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relational, interpersonal, and corrective object-relations techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques evolved for patients with severe problems of basic trust include expressing empathic attunement/warmth, limited analyst self-disclosure, allowing patient autonomy/disagreement, and explaining others' motivations (interpersonal/intersubjective/relational approaches).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corrective relational moves are especially applicable for histories of maternal deprivation or severe object relations pathology and may supplement or replace classical interpretive work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supportive therapy techniques for deficits in ego functioning
rubrics_metrics.description: Ego-psychological refinements produce supportive techniques: discussing reality, encouragement to stay alive (including hospitalization), psychotropic medicines to relieve overwhelming affect or fantasies, and advice about meanings of things to counter abstraction failures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supportive techniques are used particularly with psychotic or near-psychotic patients who cannot tolerate full analytic interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analytic neutrality versus participation (role of silence)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Analytic Neutrality' refers to the analyst's position of not taking sides in the patient's internal struggles; it does not mean silence. The 'participant-observer' stance recognizes that the analyst inevitably interacts, favoring detailed inquiry (noting omissions/obfuscation and asking careful questions) as an alternative to pure interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate neutrality with passivity; active interventions (Arlow-style) interpret resistances and defenses; detailed inquiry can open dialogue when interpretation is less productive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation to children: play, art, and storytelling techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychoanalytic constructs are adapted for children via play therapy, art therapy, and storytelling. Using toys/games, children symbolically demonstrate fears, fantasies, and defenses; in art therapy a counselor may have a child draw a portrait and tell a story while watching for recurring themes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These child techniques are analogous to free association in adults and useful for revealing defenses like disobedience and withdrawal; they are especially applicable to preadolescent populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural adaptation requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychoanalysis can be adapted to different cultures provided the therapist understands the client's culture; the use of certain defense mechanisms may relate to cultural values, and therapy structure may need to be modified for some cultures (e.g., more structure in many Asian cultures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Therapists may need to help clients develop a cultural identity as well as an ego identity; empirical findings (e.g., Thai sample) show cultural variance in defense mechanism expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment duration, frequency, and modality selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Classical analysis commonly requires sessions three to five times per week and may last on average 5.7 years; modified dynamic therapies and certain group therapies are less frequent (once–three times/week). Brief therapies (BRT, BPT, TLDP) limit treatment to 20–30 sessions; brief relational/intensive short-term dynamic therapies have reported different effect sizes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select modality and duration based on severity, ego/object relations deficits, symptom complexity, character pathology, patient resources, and insurance coverage; longer analyses indicated for more serious disturbances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training standards and supervisory requirements for analysts
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical U.S. psychoanalytic training: personal analytic treatment for trainee, ~600 hours of class instruction over about four years, weekly supervision on each analytic case, minimum number of analytic cases (often two to four, including male and female cases), and extended supervision over years. Entry qualifications often include a terminal degree (Ph.D., Psy.D., M.S.W., or M.D.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many training centers are accredited by APA/IPA committees; supervision occurs in the supervisor's office and trainees present weekly case material and receive technique instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organizational accreditation, ethics, and continuing education
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizations like the International Psychoanalytical Association (IPA) and national societies (e.g., British Psychoanalytical Society) set procedures/models for practice, training, and ethical standards (e.g., Codes of Ethics), and promote continuing professional development through conferences, publications, and registers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership and accreditation signal adherence to accepted educational, ethical, and practice standards; societies publish journals and maintain libraries to further theory and research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards and evidence for evaluating effectiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical evaluations (meta-analyses and systematic reviews) show mixed results: some meta-analyses report psychoanalysis/psychodynamic therapies more effective than no treatment and than shorter forms; others (e.g., Cochrane review) found no data demonstrating effectiveness for schizophrenia and cautioned use only alongside medication. Reported effect sizes vary widely across STPP, I-STPP, LTPP, and disorder-specific reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret evidence cautiously: methodologies have been criticized, effectiveness appears diagnosis- and therapist-dependent, and some reviews (INSERM, APA comparisons) yield nuanced conclusions about which disorders show benefit (e.g., panic disorder, PTSD, personality disorders) and which do not (e.g., schizophrenia, sex offenders).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criticisms and scientific rigor requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Major criticisms concern lack of empirical verification, reliance on qualitative case studies, and theoretical bases more aligned with interpretive phenomenology than scientific positivism. Historical controversies (e.g., seduction hypothesis, infantile sexuality) and allegations of methodological shortcomings have driven calls for more rigorous, quantitative research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ongoing integration with attachment theory and empirical research (e.g., prospective studies, validated measures) is necessary to address criticisms; recognize that some psychoanalytic concepts (unconscious, transference) have received empirical investigation in cognitive and social psychology.
